$comment: Everyday stories for the capabilities catalogue (docs/DSL_CAPABILITIES.html), owner request 2026-11-22: for EACH keyword a short story in plain, daily language that a non-technical person can hold on to -- what situation the keyword answers and what the platform then does. Style: a real person or place in the first sentence, the problem in the second, what the keyword does in the third; no jargon, no code in the story (the real JSON example sits beside it); at most ~70 words; the story must not promise anything the keyword's technical meaning does not say. Key = the slot id exactly as the catalogue shows it (`<def>.<property>`, `pack:<property>`, `root:<property>`); the generator refuses a story for a keyword the schema does not have. This file is the PILOT (17 of 785): the owner judges the tone before the rest are written.

stories.field.required: At a clinic's front desk, someone books an appointment and forgets to write down the patient's name. Now nobody knows who is coming. Marking a box as required is the thick red star on a paper form: NPDev will not save the booking until that box is filled in, and it says so right there, while the person is still typing.
stories.field.unique: Two customers can share a name, but never a tax number: if they did, one person's invoice could land in another person's mailbox. Unique means no two records may carry the same value in this box. The moment someone tries to repeat one, NPDev refuses and says which record already has it.
stories.field.maxLength: The warehouse label printer fits 30 letters per line, and a product called 'Extra-soft hypoallergenic cotton towel, white, pack of twelve' gets cut in the middle of a word. Maximum length sets how many characters a text may have, so the app tells the person while they type, instead of the printer cutting the name later.
stories.field.sensitive: A pharmacy keeps its customers' ID numbers. Only a few people should ever see them, and nobody wants one to slip into a report, a log or a message sent to an AI. Sensitive is a 'handle with care' sticker on the box: NPDev hides the value everywhere, even from administrators, unless a rule on that box explicitly says who may read it.
stories.field.derivedExpression: On a restaurant bill nobody types the total; typing it is how mistakes happen. A derived box is filled in by NPDev itself from the other boxes, with a one-line formula such as quantity times unit price. The answer is always consistent with the numbers beside it, and nobody can type over it by hand.
stories.field.defaultExpression: When a clerk opens a new invoice, its number and today's date should already be there, so nobody has to look up what comes next. A default expression is the rule that fills a box when the person leaves it empty, for example 'the next invoice number'. If the clerk types something, theirs wins. It only applies when the record is created.
stories.field.enumValues: A ride can be Requested, Accepted, Completed or Cancelled, and nothing else, however someone spells it. Allowed values turn a free-text box into a short drop-down list. Reports can then count rides by status without surprises from 'complet' or 'Done', and nobody can invent a fifth state by mistake.
stories.field.reference: An order belongs to a customer. Instead of retyping the customer's name and address in every order, the order holds a note that says 'see card 42', and a reference is that note. Fix the address once and every order shows it. It also stops anyone pointing at a customer that does not exist.
stories.fieldConvention.match: In a family, 'birthday' always means a date and 'phone' always means a number to dial, and nobody explains it each time. A naming convention teaches NPDev the same habit: any box whose name ends in 'Dt' is a date, so you write birthDt and skip the type. Fewer words to write means fewer to get wrong.
stories.concept.lifecycle: A parcel goes from packed to shipped to delivered, and it never jumps from delivered back to packed. A lifecycle lists the stages of a record and the moves allowed between them. NPDev then refuses every other move, and buttons that would break the order simply do not appear.
stories.concept.access: In a clinic, each doctor should open their own patients' files, not everybody's. Access rules say, record by record, who may read or change what, for example 'only the doctor assigned to this patient'. The rule lives with the data, so it holds on every screen and every call to the app, not only where someone remembered to add a check.
stories.concept.indexes: A shop with 200,000 orders has to find 'all orders of customer 4711' in a blink. An index is the alphabetical tab of an address book: the database jumps to the right page instead of reading every page. NPDev already adds them for ids and unique boxes; this keyword is for the extra ones you know people will search by.
stories.role.concepts: A cashier can create sales but not delete them; a manager can do both. A role is a job title plus a list: for each kind of record, what that job may do, such as read, create, update or delete. People are given roles, never one-off permissions, so when someone changes jobs you change one thing.
stories.experience.for: A driver and a dispatcher open the same app but need different front doors: the driver wants one big 'Go online' button on a phone, the dispatcher wants a busy board on a desk screen. An experience says which roles it is for and where they land. The first one that matches a person's role is the one they see.
stories.flow.trigger: A motion-sensor light turns itself on because something happened, not because anyone pressed a switch. A trigger does the same for a flow: it starts when an event happens (a ride is completed), on a timetable (every night at 2 a.m.) or when another system calls in (a payment confirmation), so no one has to remember to start it.
stories.flow.runAs: A rider may rate a driver, but riders must never be allowed to edit a driver's profile. Updating the driver's average rating therefore has to run with the platform's own permission. 'Run as' says whose permissions a flow uses: the person who pressed the button (the default) or the system. The person who asked is still written down.
stories.flow.expose: Some flows are the public door ('book a table' on a website), some sit behind a button on a screen, and some are private helpers that only other flows may call. Expose decides who may start a flow at all, so a helper that charges a card can never be started by a stranger who guesses its address.
